note: Life-transition simulations. Each simulation is a staged narrative layered on top of an existing capstone assessment item. The simulation NEVER changes how evidence is recorded: the learner still answers the capstone task, the engine still judges it against the same per-subskill scoring rows, and evidence is still stored per subskill exactly as before. What the simulation adds is a realistic frame: progressive disclosure of information, a mid-situation change of constraint, and explicit trade-offs. It lives beside capstones.json rather than inside it so the assessment bank and the evidence model stay untouched.

simulations.title: Moving out in six weeks
simulations.promise: Plan a move you can actually afford, then keep it working when the plan breaks.
simulations.framing: Six weeks from now you want to be living somewhere of your own. Everything below is fictional.
simulations.setting: You have a job and a move date that is not moving. You have found two places and neither is quite what you hoped.

stages.heading: The two options
stages.beat: Compare what they cost, not what they advertise.
reveal: Option A: rent 600 a month, utilities about 140, transport 120. Upfront: 600 rent, 600 deposit, 150 moving costs. Last bus 20:15; your shifts sometimes run to 21:00.
Option B: rent 700 a month, utilities about 100, transport 40. Upfront: 700 rent, 700 deposit, 100 moving costs. The walking route has not been checked for step-free access.
Take-home income: 1,500 a month. Other essentials: food 220, phone 25, debt payment 80. You have 1,550 saved for moving costs, separate from your monthly budget.
stages.ask: Work out the full monthly cost of each, including the things that are easy to forget. Then compare them against your actual income — and say which details you do not yet know that could change the answer.
stages.trap: The cheaper rent is not automatically the cheaper option. Check what each one quietly costs you in time and money.

stages.heading: What is actually in the paperwork
stages.beat: Read for what is missing, not just what is present.
reveal: Option A's tenancy agreement has a repairs clause you have not read. Option B's has no clear cancellation or notice wording.
Neither landlord has confirmed who handles the boiler if it fails.
stages.ask: What would you ask each landlord before you paid anything? Write the questions, not the answers you assume.
stages.trap: An unanswered question is not a 'no problem'. It is an unknown you are choosing to take on.

stages.heading: A change of plan
reveal: Your hours have been cut: your take-home income is now 1,250 a month.
Option B's step-free route has been closed for a week of essential repairs.
stages.ask: Revise your monthly budget and your transport plan. Does your decision change? If it does, is there a reversible way to make it?
stages.trap: The person who made the earlier decision without new information will often make the same one again. Decide deliberately, as if from scratch.

records: Where will you keep your deposit, your tenancy agreement, and your ID — and can you get to them quickly?
What is your first-week food, cleaning and laundry plan?
If the boiler or the heating failed in week one, what would you do first?
simulations.debrief: A move is not one decision. It is a comparison, a set of commitments, a set of records, and a plan for the week something goes wrong. You have now made each of those under pressure.

simulations.title: Your first job
simulations.promise: Handle a job, a payslip and the paperwork — starting from the offer.
simulations.framing: Everything is fictional. No real employer, no real contract.
simulations.setting: You have been offered a job. It is your first, and you do not want to agree to something you do not understand.

stages.heading: The offer
stages.beat: Read it as a set of facts.
reveal: Hourly rate 12.10. Shifts of 4 hours, 5 days a week. 'Standard' holiday mentioned but not defined.
You are asked to confirm within 3 days, and the person messaging you will not answer questions until you agree.
stages.ask: What is actually promised, what is undefined, and what would you ask before confirming? Is the pressure itself a warning sign?
stages.trap: Urgency and 'we can't discuss until you commit' are information, not just obstacles.

stages.heading: Your first payslip
reveal: Basic pay 484.00. A 'service charge deduction' of 61.76 appears with no line explaining it. Tax 40.02. Net pay 374.98.
stages.ask: Do these numbers add up correctly? Which figure would you query, and to whom, in writing?
stages.trap: An unexplained deduction is a normal-looking item on a real payslip. Checking is expected, not rude.

stages.heading: It changes again
stages.beat: The deduction is not the problem you have to solve today.
reveal: Three of your shifts were not paid, and the unexplained service charge is still on the payslip.
You have now been in the job for two weeks, and a colleague tells you the same charge appears for everyone — but nobody has seen it in writing.
stages.ask: Which of these do you raise first, and why? What would you put in writing, and what would you wait to be asked about before you say it?
stages.trap: Raising every possible problem at once can get a real one ignored. Naming the unpaid shifts and the missing hours first is what gets those paid.

records: Where will you record shifts worked and pay received?
What proof do you have of your agreement (offer, hours, rate)?
simulations.debrief: A job is an offer you can check, pay you can reconcile, evidence you can keep, and a problem you can raise. You have now done all four.

simulations.title: An unexpected £300
simulations.promise: Absorb a real shock to your budget before it becomes a crisis.
simulations.setting: You have been managing, roughly. Then something arrives that you did not plan for.

stages.heading: The shock
stages.beat: Size it honestly before you react.
reveal: Your boiler has failed. A quote of 300 to repair, due in 14 days. You have about 90 in savings.
Your monthly budget has been tight since you started tracking it.
stages.ask: What are your real options, including the option of not borrowing? What would each one actually cost you?
stages.trap: The first number that feels like 'the answer' is often a credit offer dressed as a solution.

stages.heading: The offers
reveal: Option 1: pay £300 from savings — you cannot, you have 90. Option 2: a 'flexible' loan, 300 over 12 months at a high rate. Option 3: an instalment plan with the supplier.
stages.ask: Compare what each actually costs in total, not monthly. Which is the least reversible? What would you need to check before any of them?
stages.trap: A monthly figure that looks affordable can hide a large total cost. Compare totals.

stages.heading: It changes again
stages.beat: The plan you chose is now under new pressure.
reveal: You took the instalment plan. Two weeks later your hours are cut, and the first payment is due on a Friday you do not get paid until Monday.
You now have 41 in savings instead of 90, and the supplier will charge a missed-payment fee.
stages.ask: What do you do before the payment is missed rather than after? Who do you contact first, what exactly do you say, and what evidence do you need to keep?
stages.trap: Missing a payment and then calling is the expensive version. Contacting the provider before it is missed, with your agreement to hand, is the cheap version.

records: Where will you keep proof of the quotes, the loan or plan terms, and what you paid?
simulations.debrief: An unexpected cost is survivable if you can size it, compare the real options, keep the evidence, and change something so it happens less expensively next time.

simulations.title: A suspicious payment request
simulations.promise: Tell a real request from a fake one, and act before it costs you.
simulations.framing: Fictional scenario. Never act on real financial requests without verifying through a route the requester did not give you.
simulations.setting: A message arrives that looks routine and is not.

stages.heading: The request
reveal: A 'supplier' messages you to say your payment did not go through and asks you to pay by bank transfer within the hour. They include your company name and last order.
stages.ask: What tells you this might not be genuine? What is the single most important thing you will do first — and what will you deliberately not do?
stages.trap: Having your real details and being in a hurry are designed to stop you checking. Urgency plus a private channel is itself a red flag.

stages.heading: The check
reveal: You find a phone number on an invoice you already had and call it. The real supplier says they never asked you to change payment details.
stages.ask: How did you verify without using anything the requester gave you? What would you do now — to the account, the message, and the record?
stages.trap: Calling a number in the message is not verification — the scammer controls it. Verify through a route you already trusted.

stages.heading: Protecting next time
reveal: You avoided the loss. Now consider what made you a target and what would make you less so.
stages.ask: What is one change that would make the next attempt harder — to your account, your backup access, or how requests are confirmed?
stages.trap: The strongest protection is a safe backup you already have before you need it, not one you set up in a panic.

records: How will you keep a record of a suspicious contact, and what have you already set up to protect the account that protects everything else?
simulations.debrief: Scams rely on urgency, secrecy and real-looking details. You can break all three by pausing, verifying through a route the requester did not choose, and keeping evidence.

simulations.title: The week that overloaded
simulations.promise: Plan a realistic week — and decide what to drop when it stops being possible.
simulations.framing: Fictional. This is about prioritisation, not about working harder.
simulations.setting: Everything is due, at once, and you cannot do all of it well.

stages.heading: Everything at once
stages.beat: See the real shape of the week.
reveal: An assignment due in 5 days. A shift pattern change for next week. A bill you forgot about. A call you have been avoiding. You have about 20 free hours across the week.
stages.ask: What genuinely has to happen, by when, for the worst outcome? What are you assuming has to happen that actually does not?
stages.trap: The task that feels most urgent is often not the one with the real deadline.

stages.heading: Revising that does not stick
reveal: You have read the material three times. You still could not answer a question about it.
stages.ask: What is different about testing yourself than reading again? What is one thing you could do in 20 minutes that would tell you whether you actually know it?
stages.trap: Familiarity from re-reading feels like knowledge. It is not the same as being able to recall and apply.

stages.heading: The week changed
stages.beat: New information, and less time than you counted on.
reveal: Your shift pattern has changed: you now work two extra hours on Thursday, and Friday is no longer free at all.
That leaves 13 free hours, not 20 — and the assignment is due in 2 days rather than 5, because the deadline moved.
The bill you forgot about is also due in 2 days.
stages.ask: With 13 hours and a 2-day deadline, what do you drop, and what do you tell each person? What would you negotiate rather than simply abandon?
stages.trap: Working out what is still possible from the plan you made on Monday is the failure mode. The plan is now wrong; recompute, do not catch up.

records: How will you track what is due and when you last actually practised each skill?
simulations.debrief: Staying on top of a busy week is not about trying harder. It is about knowing what matters, revising by testing yourself, and deciding openly what to drop.
